subtitle: One project, from git init to push
description: Git from zero: 12 picture cards with native audio, the traps people actually fall into, real questions and 24 version-control words.

spine.title: The route
spine.note: One project in order: create the repo, work and track changes, save snapshots, branch out, share with others.

explain.title: The big picture
explain.why: Git is a time machine for your files. Every commit is a snapshot you can return to, compare or hand to someone else — and none of it needs the internet.

tiles.en: Staging picks the changes for you
A short hash names every commit
Branches let ideas grow apart safely
Two edits, one line — you choose

cards.alt: A terminal window running git init
cards.ko: git init turns this folder into a repository that Git can watch.
cards.en: git init — run once in the project root

cards.alt: A folder with a hidden .git tag
cards.ko: Everything Git remembers lives inside one hidden folder called .git.
cards.en: Delete .git and all history is gone — the files stay

cards.alt: A magnifier over a list of changed files
cards.ko: When you are lost, run git status — it says where you are and what changed.

cards.alt: Two pages showing removed and added lines
cards.ko: git diff shows every line that changed before you decide anything.

cards.alt: A file being placed into an inbox tray
cards.ko: git add puts changes in the staging area — the waiting list for the next snapshot.
cards.en: git add login.py (or git add . for everything)

cards.alt: A polaroid snapshot with a green check
cards.ko: git commit saves the staged changes as one snapshot, with a message that says why.

cards.alt: A vertical timeline of commit dots
cards.ko: git log walks you backwards through every snapshot, newest first.

cards.alt: A curved back arrow around a file
cards.ko: Undo is never scary here: git restore brings a file back from the last snapshot.
cards.en: git restore login.py · undo a commit: git reset --soft HEAD~1

cards.alt: A line of commits forking into a second line
cards.ko: A branch is its own line of work, so an experiment can't break main.

cards.alt: Two commit lines joining at one point
cards.ko: Merging folds one branch's snapshots into another; a conflict is just Git asking who wins.
cards.en: git switch main · git merge new-feature

cards.alt: A cloud holding a repository folder
cards.ko: A remote is the shared copy of your repo, usually on GitHub — everyone's work lives there.
cards.en: origin = the default name of your remote

cards.alt: A laptop exchanging arrows with a cloud
cards.ko: Clone copies a whole repo with history; push sends your commits out; pull brings other people's in.
cards.en: git clone <url> · git push · git pull --rebase

qa_note: Start with the traps — they are where most Git fear comes from.

items.q: I ran git add . and committed everything — including my secrets.
items.a: Untrack it now: git rm --cached .env, put it in .gitignore, commit. If the repo was ever pushed, rotate the secret — history keeps old copies forever.
items.why: Staging is a promise about what belongs in the snapshot; add . promises everything.

items.q: I work straight on main because branching feels like extra work.
items.a: Open a branch before every change: git switch -c fix-login. Merging your own small branch takes seconds and keeps mistakes off main.
items.why: main stays clean and reviewable; an accident stays quarantined on its side line.

items.q: I thought git pull just downloads files.
items.a: Pull downloads other people's commits AND merges them into your work — that is where conflicts come from. Use git fetch to look first, merge when ready.
items.why: Download and integrate are two steps; pull quietly does both at once.

items.q: I deleted a commit by mistake — it is gone forever?
items.a: Almost never. git reflog lists every position HEAD has held; find the old hash and reset hard back to it.
items.why: Git rarely deletes commits quickly — it moves pointers, and reflog remembers them.

items.q: How do I undo my last commit but keep the changes?
items.a: git reset --soft HEAD~1 — the commit disappears and your changes wait in the staging area.
HEAD is where you are right now: which branch, on which commit. Undo commands are really about moving it.

items.q: My push was rejected. What now?
items.a: The remote has commits you don't. Run git pull --rebase, fix any conflicts, then git push again.

items.q: A merge conflict appeared. Walk me through it.
items.a: Open the marked files, keep the lines you want, delete Git's marker lines, then git add each file and commit.

items.q: How do I stop tracking a file without deleting it?
items.a: Run git rm --cached for that file, add it to .gitignore, commit. The file stays on your disk.
items.aen: git rm --cached <file> · then list it in .gitignore

items.ko: Read git status again — it usually names the exact next command.
items.en: Git's own hint line is the map.

items.ko: git log --oneline --graph --all shows where every branch really is.
items.en: See the whole map before touching anything.

items.ko: git reflog finds commits you thought were lost.
items.en: The safety net for undo disasters.

items.ko: Type git help, then any command name, to read its manual page offline.
items.en: The docs live in your terminal.

full.title: Start · Make a repo
full.ko: git init turns this folder into a repository that Git can watch. Everything Git remembers lives inside one hidden folder called .git.
full.en: git init — run once in the project root Delete .git and all history is gone — the files stay

full.title: Work · Track changes
full.ko: When you are lost, run git status — it says where you are and what changed. git diff shows every line that changed before you decide anything. git add puts changes in the staging area — the waiting list for the next snapshot.
full.en: git status git diff · git diff --staged git add login.py (or git add . for everything)

full.title: Save · Commit snapshots
full.ko: git commit saves the staged changes as one snapshot, with a message that says why. git log walks you backwards through every snapshot, newest first. Undo is never scary here: git restore brings a file back from the last snapshot.
full.en: git commit -m "fix login timeout" git log --oneline --graph git restore login.py · undo a commit: git reset --soft HEAD~1

full.title: Branch · Parallel work
full.ko: A branch is its own line of work, so an experiment can't break main. Merging folds one branch's snapshots into another; a conflict is just Git asking who wins.
full.en: git switch -c new-feature git switch main · git merge new-feature

full.title: Share · Push and pull
full.ko: A remote is the shared copy of your repo, usually on GitHub — everyone's work lives there. Clone copies a whole repo with history; push sends your commits out; pull brings other people's in.
full.en: origin = the default name of your remote git clone <url> · git push · git pull --rebase
